stories.head: Loft Orbital partners with NASA for AI tests
stories.body: Loft Orbital is teaming up with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory to test AI models on its spacecraft, aimed at enhancing Earth observation capabilities. The collaboration underscores a growing trend where satellites are increasingly relying on artificial intelligence to process data more efficiently. Expect more companies to follow suit as the data deluge continues.
stories.soWhat: If satellites start thinking for themselves, the entire data analytics game might shift from mere collection to real-time insights.

stories.head: Palantir secures $480M extension on TITAN program
stories.body: Palantir has landed a $480 million extension for its TITAN ground station program, a significant boost that reflects the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to enhancing its data processing capabilities. This extension is part of a broader trend of defense contracts favoring firms that can deliver robust analytics solutions under tight timelines.
stories.soWhat: In government contracts, it seems that being slow and steady is just as winning as being fast and flashy.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M for co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly has successfully raised $190 million in a Series C funding round, pushing its valuation to $1.6 billion. This funding will bolster its efforts in co-orbital security and space domain awareness, areas that are becoming increasingly vital as geopolitical tensions rise. The company is positioning itself well in a market that is seeing heightened demand for security solutions.
stories.soWhat: When co-orbital threats are on the rise, investors are betting that security in space will be the next gold rush.

talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
